{"id": "20:14/q21", "question": "What reports describe the Prophet's missed prayers and their performance?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted episodes and the number of prayers missed.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q21/p1", "position": "After the Trench, the Prophet made up ʿAṣr after sunset, then prayed Maghrib.", "reasons": "Jābir's report is in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections and is preferred by al-Qurṭubī as explicit evidence of order; ʿUmar also had missed ʿAṣr."}, {"id": "20:14/q21/p2", "position": "At the Trench, the Prophet made up four prayers in order: noon, afternoon, sunset, night.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī reports this through Abū ʿUbayda from his father."}, {"id": "20:14/q21/p3", "position": "The Prophet's party slept past sunrise, moved, and made up dawn prayer.", "reasons": "Abū Qatāda reports moving the mounts before prayer; ʿImrān reports two rakʿahs and Fajr after travel. Abū Hurayra describes a post-Khaybar night when Bilāl slept on watch, then the party moved, performed ablution and prayed. Ibn Masʿūd gives a return-from-Hudaybiyya episode; Abū Juḥayfa reports God returning their souls."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q22", "question": "How does this declaration of oneness relate to salvation and ʿUmar's conversion?", "turns_on": "Distinct reports about the declaration's reception and virtue.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q22/p1", "position": "Sincere testimony to God's oneness promises safety from punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports a gate of Paradise bearing the promise; ʿAlī transmits a divine report through Gabriel describing the testimony as entry to God's fortress."}, {"id": "20:14/q22/p2", "position": "ʿUmar embraced Islam after reading Ṭā Hā including this declaration.", "reasons": "Anas recounts the event and Khabbāb's recollection of the Prophet's prayer that Islam be strengthened through ʿUmar or ʿAmr ibn Hishām."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q23", "question": "What inward experience is sought through remembrance and prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the experience is described as enduring presence or direct witnessing beyond attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q23/p1", "position": "Remain wholly present with God in proper adab and intimate communion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ warns against heedlessness in turning to God. Al-Wāsiṭī says no deed or word should displace Him from the heart and one should transcend passing times. Al-Qushayrī says witnessing another as the true establisher opens intimate nearness, while praying unaware of the Originator yields self-admiration. Al-Bursawī cites lasting converse, theophany and annihilation; Rūzbihān describes the servant becoming remembrance amid disclosure of divine secrets and beauty."}, {"id": "20:14/q23/p2", "position": "Prayer is spiritual witnessing of the Essence beyond the heart's remembrance of attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī distinguishes essential witnessing from presence of heart with divine attributes; al-Qushayrī says forms and traces vanish before the Real's existence."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q24", "question": "How is this verse ordered with the surrounding address and wider prophetic teaching?", "turns_on": "How broadly the surrounding revelation is included in the sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q24/p1", "position": "Knowledge of oneness comes first, then worship and prayer, then the Hereafter and mission.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says doctrine precedes practical branches and lists six charges to Moses: oneness, worship/prayer, Hereafter, wisdom of God's acts, signs and mission. Al-Bursawī makes creed prior to practice. Al-Ālūsī maps beginning, middle and return across 20:14–15; Ibn ʿĀshūr traces command, Hour, warning and ruin. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees monotheism and resurrection explicit, prophecy implicit, worship condensing practice; he locates the mission between the staff question and Pharaoh command and compares 19:51. Iṣlāḥī identifies three founding duties given to all messengers."}, {"id": "20:14/q24/p2", "position": "The sequence begins in unity and ends in prayerful obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī emphasizes the move from divine oneness to the language of obedience."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q25", "question": "What is said about prayer in Moses' scriptural legacy?", "turns_on": "Whether Torah prayer references preserve Mosaic instruction or later editing.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q25/p1", "position": "Moses was directed first to prayer after monotheism, though later Jews neglected prayer and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī aligns this with prophetic history, notes Torah reference to temple prayer only once in Deuteronomy 26, and says Jewish scriptures speak more often of sacrifice."}, {"id": "20:14/q25/p2", "position": "Some Jewish jurists say Moses never commanded prayer and later Torah editors added its mention.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī reports this view without endorsing it."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q26", "question": "What adjacent reading and message introduce Moses' reception of this verse?", "turns_on": "Variant wording in the preceding address, with no substantive disagreement in meaning according to al-Ṭabarī.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q26/p1", "position": "The doubled-nūn, open-alif reading links selection to the earlier call to Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī attributes this reading of the preceding selection statement to the general Kufan readers and accepts it as sound."}, {"id": "20:14/q26/p2", "position": "The light-nūn reading states God's selection of Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī attributes it to most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans, accepts both readings because their meanings agree, and says Moses was chosen for the message, then told to listen, retain and act."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q27", "question": "What contextual linguistic principles do the cited discussions bring to this passage?", "turns_on": "These notes discuss different linguistic and theological context rather than competing answers.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q27/p1", "position": "Figurative expressions retain a connection to their literal source.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī warns that forcing a literal hand into al-Shammākh's right-hand phrase makes it trivial; al-Khansāʾ's hand toward glory corresponds to receiving its banner. Severing figurative names from their source breeds strained readings; 50:37 depicts incomprehension as deprivation of a heart, not a bare synonym for intellect, as with sight and hearing."}, {"id": "20:14/q27/p2", "position": "The preceding divine istiwāʾ is best understood as power.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī prefers Abū ʿAlī's interpretation and calls the Kullābī act-or-attribute account unintelligible."}, {"id": "20:14/q27/p3", "position": "A pronoun of affair needs explanation by a clause, and differing sentence moods can be conjoined.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī says an otherwise unexplained impersonal pronoun needs a following word or clause; the pronoun of affair takes a clause, unlike singular pronouns of niʿma and biʾsa. He reports Ibn Kharūf, al-Ṣaffār and Ibn ʿAmr permitting conjunction of imperative, report and prohibition."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q28", "question": "Which early explanations of the prayer command are transmitted?", "turns_on": "Whether remembrance denotes God during prayer or recollection of an owed prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q28/p1", "position": "Mujāhid says prayer brings remembrance of the Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī transmits Mujāhid's concise formulation; Ibn Kathīr reports the same interpretation without naming its proponent."}, {"id": "20:14/q28/p2", "position": "Ibrāhīm says to pray upon remembering an omitted prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī transmits this early interpretation."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q29", "question": "How does divine reality relate to beginnings and passing time?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q29/p1", "position": "Beginnings, ends, times and epochs limit creatures but not God's reality.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ draws this inward implication from the verse."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q01", "question": "What does the interrogative mā ask Moses to tell?", "turns_on": "Whether mā seeks the object's name, its qualities and uses, or both; Tabatabai invokes the feminine demonstrative and Moses' detailed reply.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q01/p1", "position": "It asks him to identify the object in his hand as his staff.", "reasons": "Tabari, Wahidi al-Wajiz, Razi reporting al-Zajjaj and al-Farra, Asad, and Wahb transmitted by Suyuti present the question as identification. Zarkashi says interrogative mā asks about the objects, kinds, or qualities of non-rational things and can also ask the kinds or qualities of rational beings (2:68, 2:69). Bursawi says it asks the thing's essence, as asking what Zayd is and answering that he is a human."}, {"id": "20:17/q01/p2", "position": "It asks about the known staff's qualities and uses, rather than merely its name.", "reasons": "Jishumi compares asking about Dhu al-Qarnayn to elicit his story (18:83); Razi and Alusi say Moses then learns uses beyond human reason's grasp (20:18). Tabatabai argues the feminine تلك points to the already known staff: an unknown thing would have been indicated with masculine ذلك; he prefers asking for its qualities, explaining why Moses lists uses."}, {"id": "20:17/q01/p3", "position": "It invites both identification of the staff and a description of its ordinary benefits.", "reasons": "Baydawi says Moses understood both parts of the invitation and named the staff and its uses before its transformation. Tabatabai says the reply establishes that it was lifeless matter. Zarkashi says Moses' answer matches the question and adds information."}]}

Basran grammarians restrict relative use of demonstratives to dhā under conditions; Abu al-Abbas rejects relative use of demonstratives altogether."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q03", "question": "How is mā tilka bi-yamīnika parsed?", "turns_on": "The subject-predicate order and whether bi-yamīnika is circumstantial or a relative complement; the Kufan and Basran rules for demonstratives divide the latter analyses.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q03/p1", "position": "Mā is the interrogative subject, tilka its predicate, and bi-yamīnika is circumstantial or governed by the demonstrative's pointing.", "reasons": "Nahhas calls it a subject-predicate sentence. Kashshaf compares the circumstantial pointing with 11:72; Tabarsi's later grammarian says the circumstantial phrase specifies the demonstrative and avoids modifying it by an indefinite clause. Baydawi also allows this attachment; Nasafi says the staff rests in or is held by the hand. Abu Hayyan and Samin explicitly assign subject and predicate. Alusi explains an omitted circumstantial predicate and says this is one permissible ordering."}, {"id": "20:17/q03/p2", "position": "Tilka is the subject and interrogative mā its predicate.", "reasons": "Bursawi says the predicate is the question about the thing's essence, and this order better fits Moses' answer; Alusi likewise considers both orders and finds this one better suited to the meaning and reply."}, {"id": "20:17/q03/p3", "position": "Tilka functions as a relative expression completed by bi-yamīnika, ‘the thing in your right hand.’", "reasons": "Al-Farra cites a line by Yazid ibn Mufarrigh or Yazid ibn Rabi'a, using a demonstrative for ‘the one you carry’; his account explains ʿadas as a mule-shooing cry. Tabari says demonstratives join complements as alladhī does. Zajjaj calls tilka an indefinite demonstrative-like noun behaving as allatī. Nahhas says Abu Ishaq leaned toward al-Farra. Alusi describes Ibn Atiyya's omitted relative clause. Abu Hayyan identifies this as Kufan rather than Basran; Samin states the schools' opposing rules. Abu al-Abbas objects that demonstratives cannot be relatives, and Tabarsi's later grammarian objects that an indefinite clause cannot describe an ambiguous demonstrative."}, {"id": "20:17/q03/p4", "position": "Mā itself is a relative noun linked to bi-yamīnika.", "reasons": "Qurtubi attributes this analysis to Zajjaj and al-Farra and glosses it as ‘what is the thing in your right hand?’ This differs in which word is treated as relative."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q04", "question": "What does yamīn mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether yamīn specifically names the right hand or can denote either hand in Arabic usage.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q04/p1", "position": "It means Moses' right hand.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives this as a possible sense of yamīn and compares 69:19. Nasafi describes the staff as resting in or held by it."}, {"id": "20:17/q04/p2", "position": "It means a hand, whether right or left.", "reasons": "Islahi appeals to classical Arabic usage."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q05", "question": "Why specify Moses' hand as bi-yamīnika?", "turns_on": "The notes explain the precision through possible multiple objects, Moses' confusion, or the coming sign involving the hand itself.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q05/p1", "position": "It identifies exactly which object is being asked about.", "reasons": "Bursawi suggests Moses could have held a ring or another item in the left hand, making an unspecific ‘in your hand’ unclear."}, {"id": "20:17/q05/p2", "position": "It helps a bewildered Moses distinguish right from left.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports that the wonders had left him confused enough to need this specification."}, {"id": "20:17/q05/p3", "position": "It sets Moses' hand alongside the staff as a separate sign.", "reasons": "Razi says those two things are separately indicated and each becomes an overpowering sign, with inert matter elevated to a miraculous state."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q06", "question": "Why address Moses again by name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q06/p1", "position": "Repeating his name increases familiarity and draws his attention.", "reasons": "Baydawi gives both effects of the direct address."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q07", "question": "Why does God ask about the staff when He already knows it?", "turns_on": "The question's proposed function: certify the staff before the miracle, secure Moses' admission, soothe his fear, teach unknown uses, focus attention, or invite extended speech.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q07/p1", "position": "To establish Moses' certainty about the ordinary staff before its miraculous transformation.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari connect the question with the coming serpent and its sign for Pharaoh. Wahidi's authorities, Ibn Atiyya, Tabarsi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Bursawi, Tabatabai and Study Quran stress Moses' recognition of dry or harmless wood before the change. Kashshaf and Bursawi compare a goldsmith displaying iron before making armor. Razi says this displays power over lowly things and makes the miracle unmistakable; Biqai also associates the swift transformation with a sign of the Hour. Qushayri says repeated questions about the staff reflect its future great miracle. Zarkashi reports that prior identification prevents surprise. Moses' response was to be knowledge in the heart and verbal acknowledgement, says Baghawi."}, {"id": "20:17/q07/p2", "position": "To obtain Moses' own admission of the staff's identity as proof against later denial.", "reasons": "Zajjaj illustrates eliciting an admission with dyed water; Wahidi's Abu Ishaq compares making a person name water before changing it. Ibn al-Jawzi reports Zajjaj's same proof argument. Qurtubi notes that God's prior knowledge is no obstacle to seeking an admission. Ibn Qutayba compares confirmation questions to those addressed to Jesus and communities by messengers."}, {"id": "20:17/q07/p3", "position": "To ease Moses' awe and fear by letting him answer a familiar, easy question.", "reasons": "Sulami reports Faris and Abu Bakr ibn Tahir: divine address nearly overwhelmed Moses, so the question returned him to created things and steadied him. Wasiti says direct speech had carried him beyond ordinary discernment. Qushayri warns that sustained awe would prevent understanding or bearing the encounter. Jishumi says ordinary human speech calmed him. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, Nasafi, Qashani, Ibn Kathir, Zarkashi, Biqai, Suyuti, and Alusi likewise give reassurance; Alusi says a correct answer restores composure. Islahi calls the tone affectionate like a parent asking a child a known answer."}, {"id": "20:17/q07/p4", "position": "To ask after the staff's uses and reveal uses beyond Moses' knowledge.", "reasons": "Jishumi says God indicated miraculous uses after Moses gave an ordinary one, and compares a question about Dhu al-Qarnayn (18:83). Razi says the question teaches the limits of human reason even about an object in one's hand (20:18); Alusi repeats the contrast between divine perfection and human limitation. Zarkashi reports Ibn Faris calling the question an imparting of unknown understanding."}, {"id": "20:17/q07/p5", "position": "To prepare Moses' attention for the important revelation and miracles ahead.", "reasons": "Nahhas identifies an alerting force; Jishumi says the prompt signals that something important is coming. Ibn Atiyya says Moses is readied to receive what follows; the divine knowledge of the object is eternal. Wahidi's authorities and Baydawi likewise speak of focused reflection and awakening to wonders."}, {"id": "20:17/q07/p6", "position": "To give Moses room to speak at length in the encounter.", "reasons": "Abu Bakr ibn Tahir says God wanted Moses to speak expansively so he would not feel constrained when asking."}]}
{"id": "20:17/q08", "question": "Why did Moses answer beyond the apparent request?", "turns_on": "Whether his fuller answer reflects delight and awe, expectation of a miracle, or the scope of the question itself.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q08/p1", "position": "The delight or awe of being addressed by God led him to extend his answer.", "reasons": "Sulami's Faris says Moses, almost overwhelmed by unprecedented speech, claimed the staff as his and said more than asked; Wasiti says pleasure in direct address impaired discernment, while the stick to Moses was already a moving serpent in divine knowledge. Qushayri says divine address itself was the greatest benefit. Suyuti says Moses added uses from delight in the conversation."}, {"id": "20:17/q08/p2", "position": "He sensed a great event involving the staff and described its ordinary uses first.", "reasons": "Zarkashi says Moses anticipated something significant and therefore added ordinary uses."}, {"id": "20:17/q08/p3", "position": "The question invited both the staff's identity and its uses.", "reasons": "Baydawi says Moses understood the invitation this way. Biqai says he first listed needs the staff served for himself, then those of his flock; Alusi suggests leaning came first because it directly answered what was in his right hand."}]}

{"id": "20:17/q11", "question": "What sign did the staff question begin, and for whom?", "turns_on": "Whether the staff sign was needed to certify Moses' prophethood to himself, or his earlier encounter at the tree already sufficed and the signs served the people.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q11/p1", "position": "The staff's transformation is a sign of God's power and a proof for Moses' mission to his people and Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari link the question to the serpent and Pharaoh. Razi says the change of inert dry wood into living, powerful matter displays divine greatness. Biqai says conviction is strengthened and recipients of the mission confirmed; Islahi calls the staff the source of Moses' miracles."}, {"id": "20:17/q11/p2", "position": "The staff and hand signs also establish Moses' prophethood for Moses himself.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports that the question was revelation because he had been commanded to listen to revelation, and a prophet needs a sign by which to know his own prophethood; the staff's effects supply it."}, {"id": "20:17/q11/p3", "position": "The tree's sign already established Moses' prophethood; staff and hand confirmed it for his people.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the tree sufficed for Moses personally. {"id": "20:17/q13", "question": "What spiritual reading is drawn from the staff and its change?", "turns_on": "The readings draw different inward correspondences: hidden reality, self under intellect, or moral change of the heart.", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q13/p1", "position": "God knows hidden realities behind the staff's outward form and reveals them to Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata says Moses knew only its appearance while God knew its transformation. Junayd says Moses knew its name and uses; disclosure of its hidden serpent reality prepared him against fear and directed him back to God (20:67). Al-Husayn says Moses' verified description and the change exposed his incapacity and furnished a communal sign."}, {"id": "20:17/q13/p2", "position": "The staff signifies the self held in the intellect's right hand.", "reasons": "Qashani says this hand receives divine gifts and restrains the self."}, {"id": "20:17/q13/p3", "position": "The staff's change mirrors God's power to transform the believer's heart.", "reasons": "Razi compares inert wood made living with a disobedient heart illuminated by knowledge; the serpent swallowing magicians' sorcery with a heart swallowing the commanding soul's magic; and Moses' blessed right hand with God's fingers turning a heart from sin's darkness to service's light."}]}

{"id": "20:17/q15", "question": "Does God's direct speech to Moses prove him superior to Muhammad?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q15/p1", "position": "No; Muhammad was also addressed by God, and his community has forms of divine address.", "reasons": "Razi rejects the inference: 53:10 indicates divine address to Muhammad though its content remained secret; Muhammad's community addresses God repeatedly in prayer and believers receive greeting and honor in the next life (36:58)."}]}

{"id": "20:17/q17", "question": "What do the additional cited poetic images illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:17/q17/p1", "position": "Poets animate natural changes through human motives, motion, laughter, and reversal.", "reasons": "Jurjani describes darkness as an enemy routed by a sword it drew; a similar poem makes dawn an ambusher and night wary, while al-Khalidi recasts dawn drawing swords and night fleeing. Ibn al-Muʿtazz makes a rose laugh in victory over a fading narcissus, reversing Ibn al-Rumi's roles; his gray hair laughs at a man's ill-fitting youthful behavior, giving a motive beyond Daʿbal's bare reversal and making the image more vivid. These notes contain no explicit link to the verse."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q01", "question": "Who speaks, and what does “it” refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q01/p1", "position": "Moses speaks; “it” points back to the object God asked about.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā identifies Moses as speaker; al-Samīn identifies the antecedent as the thing asked about."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q02", "question": "Why does Moses call it “my staff”?", "turns_on": "Whether the possessive simply identifies his relation to the staff, introduces its uses, or is spiritually reproached.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q02/p1", "position": "It identifies his possession and establishes why he carries it.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says “staff” alone would identify the object; Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say “my” locates it in his right hand and prepares for the ensuing actions."}, {"id": "20:18/q02/p2", "position": "The possessive claim is reproached because Moses does not truly own or control the staff.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn al-Jawharī, and al-Qurṭubī’s report relate the later serpent and command to cast it down to this rebuke."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q03", "question": "Where did Moses' staff come from?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on its source, transfer, and wood.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q03/p1", "position": "It descended from Paradise with Adam, passed through prophets to Shuʿayb, and came to Moses from him.", "reasons": "Tustarī calls it Paradise myrtle and mentions marriage; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it basil and a house of prophetic staffs; Jishumī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī, Bursevī/Kāshifī, and Study Quran vary in details. {"id": "20:18/q12", "question": "How does the wording govern the flock and foliage?", "turns_on": "The object may be omitted or the flock may be the direct object; the preposition is explained by the verb's sense.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q12/p1", "position": "The verb omits its foliage object while ʿalā marks the sheep who receive the leaves.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī explicitly supply the omitted leaves or trees; al-Ṭabrisī compares verb alternations."}, {"id": "20:18/q12/p2", "position": "With the sīn reading, ʿalā follows the implied sense of driving toward or over the flock.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī notes that bihā ghanamī would be expected; al-Samīn calls it inclusion of a governing verb; al-Ālūsī imagines bending over the flock as if striking."}, {"id": "20:18/q12/p3", "position": "A variant construction makes the flock the direct object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī report it; al-Ālūsī cannot identify its verb reading."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q13", "question": "How is غَنَمِى read?", "turns_on": "Readings differ over the nūn and the syntactic form.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q13/p1", "position": "The regular form leaves the nūn vocalized in the genitive construction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a group reading “my sheep” in the genitive."}, {"id": "20:18/q13/p2", "position": "Some make the nūn quiescent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya knows no justification; al-Samīn says it is not productive by analogy; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also record it."}, {"id": "20:18/q13/p3", "position": "Another vocalization makes the flock the verb's direct object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report this variant."}]}

{"id": "20:18/q17", "question": "Why does plural مَـَٔارِبُ take singular feminine أُخْرَىٰ?", "turns_on": "Explanations invoke nonrational-plural agreement, collective meaning, and verse-ending cadence.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q17/p1", "position": "Nonrational or collective plurals may take a feminine singular modifier.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Samīn and others cite parallels including 20:8, 34:10, 7:180 and 17:110; Abū al-Baqāʾ says أخر would agree with the surface plural."}, {"id": "20:18/q17/p2", "position": "The singular feminine form fits the verse endings.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī offer cadence, sometimes alongside grammatical agreement; أخر is said to be possible."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q18", "question": "What ordinary additional uses of the staff are reported?", "turns_on": "Accounts give different lists and degrees of ordinary utility.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q18/p1", "position": "It carried provisions, a waterskin, tools, or other gear.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Suddī, Wahb, Ibn ʿAbbās and later commentators give variant lists; Bursevī specifies bow, quiver, milk pail and flask."}, {"id": "20:18/q18/p2", "position": "It made shade or served as a prop for a cloak.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā reports this; Ibn ʿAbbās and Wahb describe shade from a planted staff and cloak; other lists include it."}, {"id": "20:18/q18/p3", "position": "It reached branches or drew water when a well rope was short.", "reasons": "Wahb's hooked or forked staff bends or breaks branches; Ibn ʿAbbās and other accounts say it lengthened a rope or acted as a bucket."}, {"id": "20:18/q18/p4", "position": "It herded, defended, and guarded Moses' flock and himself.", "reasons": "Sources mention turning back distant sheep, warding off predators, enemies, snakes, scorpions and vermin; some accounts make the defense miraculous."}, {"id": "20:18/q18/p5", "position": "It lit the way, kindled fire, kept company, or marked prayer time.", "reasons": "Tustarī mentions prayer time; al-Māwardī mentions kindling; al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās and others describe light, speech, or companionship."}, {"id": "20:18/q18/p6", "position": "It produced food, water, fruit, or springs.", "reasons": "Accounts differ on whether it was planted, struck the earth, grew fruit, or released springs; Ibn ʿAbbās reports several forms."}, {"id": "20:18/q18/p7", "position": "It could do other practical work such as gathering fodder or serving as a prayer aid.", "reasons": "Tustarī adds fodder; al-Māwardī mentions drawing water; al-Qurṭubī's Bedouin lists prayer, travel, warmth, crossing water and a substitute weapon."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q19", "question": "Were the staff's extraordinary uses established before the serpent sign?", "turns_on": "Ibn Kathīr questions the extraordinary preexisting-use reports because of Moses' fear.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q19/p1", "position": "Some accounts attribute extraordinary powers to it already.", "reasons": "These include light, autonomous guarding, fruit, water, movement and speech in Ibn ʿAbbās and other reports; al-Bayḍāwī says God creates the signs rather than the wood possessing inherent power."}, {"id": "20:18/q19/p2", "position": "Ibn Kathīr rejects those accounts as apparent Israelite stories.", "reasons": "He argues that if Moses knew such powers, he would not have fled when the staff became a serpent; he also groups the Adam and end-time beast claims with those stories."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q20", "question": "What previously hidden benefits does God reveal through the staff?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q20/p1", "position": "Its later miracles include becoming a serpent and striking rock and sea.", "reasons": "Tustarī, Sahl and Study Quran say Moses did not yet know these uses; al-Qushayrī calls the serpent a proof of his truth; al-Qurṭubī notes the magicians believed through the signs."}, {"id": "20:18/q20/p2", "position": "The staff's greatest benefit was occasioning God's address to Moses.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar calls that greater than all the other uses; al-Rāzī says the divine question itself disclosed an additional benefit."}, {"id": "20:18/q20/p3", "position": "The question exposes how little even prophets know of a present object.", "reasons": "Tustarī, Sahl, al-Rāzī, al-Ālūsī and Study Quran take the unknown uses as evidence of the limits of human reason beside divine knowledge."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q21", "question": "How is the staff's later transformation understood?", "turns_on": "Sources differ between the wood's ordinary incapacity, divine creation of signs, and spiritual lessons.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q21/p1", "position": "The wood has no inherent power; God creates its signs and transforms it.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī explicitly denies inherent powers; Study Quran reports al-Rāzī's account that a harmless piece of wood becomes a mighty serpent."}, {"id": "20:18/q21/p2", "position": "The humble stick displays God's power through a surprising miracle.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports an explanation that mā asks its description or kind and tilka minimizes it before the transformation; al-Kashshāf also contrasts ordinary uses with the great event."}, {"id": "20:18/q21/p3", "position": "The serpent warns against attachment to anything besides God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares it with Abraham's disavowal of false gods at 26:77 and cites an ungraded hadith about unpaid zakat wealth returning as a serpent."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q22", "question": "Why does Moses add uses after naming the staff?", "turns_on": "The sources variously read the added details as affection, gratitude, an implied question, anticipation of a miracle, or a concise account.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q22/p1", "position": "He delights in God's address and wants the conversation to last.", "reasons": "Fāris, al-Qushayrī, al-Rāzī, al-Qāshānī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Itqān and Islahi say this; a poet's wish to prolong reproach illustrates it. {"id": "20:18/q24", "question": "What readings are reported for وَلِىَ فِيهَا?", "turns_on": "Readers differ between opening and quiescence of the possessive yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q24/p1", "position": "Ḥafṣ and al-Azraq from Warsh open the yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid says this is Ḥafṣ's only opened form in his listed set; Ibn al-Jazarī counts it among al-Azraq's five open wa-lī places; al-Nasafī identifies Ḥafṣ's form."}, {"id": "20:18/q24/p2", "position": "Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, and the listed Kūfan and Syrian readers use sukūn in their stated sets.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid differentiates their other yāʾ forms: Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim."}, {"id": "20:18/q24/p3", "position": "The difference is a licensed open versus unvowelled first-person yāʾ.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt Encyclopedia describes pausal versus connected form; al-Sāmarrāʾī says vowel treatment depends on language and transmitted readings."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q25", "question": "What does the staff symbolize in inward readings?", "turns_on": "The inward readings identify the staff with different faculties and treat dependence on it differently.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q25/p1", "position": "It represents intellect used to gain spiritual perfection, and the sheep represent animal faculties.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says Moses shakes useful sciences and practical wisdom from the tree of spirit and uses the staff for stations, states and disclosures."}, {"id": "20:18/q25/p2", "position": "It represents the tranquil soul, while the flock represents limbs, senses and bodily powers.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports knowers' reading: discipline effaces illusions, brings hidden aims, and can turn disobedience to obedience, citing 25:70; the serpent can be receptive to faith, as in the Medina jinn report."}, {"id": "20:18/q25/p3", "position": "The staff represents prophetic care for people who require guidance and defense.", "reasons": "Bursevī likens Satan and ego to wolves and a lion, calls prophets shepherds, and cites Ḥāfiẓ's couplet about service to Shuʿayb."}, {"id": "20:18/q25/p4", "position": "The staff's usefulness tests whether Moses attributes gifts to himself or relies on God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says a novice abandons means and the detailed list should make Moses trust God enough to cast it away; another reading says all benefits come from God, supported by poetry."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q26", "question": "What teaching is drawn from holding or leaning on a staff?", "turns_on": "Reports and authors differ in the specific benefits and applications they emphasize.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q26/p1", "position": "Carrying a staff is prophetic or recommended even without physical need.", "reasons": "Maymūn reports Ibn ʿAbbās calling it a prophetic sunnah and sign of belief; al-Ḥasan lists six benefits, and al-Ālūsī recommends it even to someone who does not need bowstring support."}, {"id": "20:18/q26/p2", "position": "It is useful in worship, sermons, and travel.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites authentic reports of the Prophet's prayer barrier and walking stick, ʿUmar's eleven-rakʿa prayer with people leaning on staffs, Solomon and Ibn Masʿūd's preaching, consensus for preachers, Mālik's travel examples, and Arab oratory; he answers Shuʿūbiyya criticism."}, {"id": "20:18/q26/p3", "position": "It can be used as a warning or corrective object in the household.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī claims correcting wives with a staff can improve relations and cites reports about Abū Jahm, ʿUbāda's counsel, and a visible whip."}, {"id": "20:18/q26/p4", "position": "Its use can remind a believer that earthly life is a journey.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites an ascetic and a poem saying a resident carries it by choice to remember travel rather than age or weakness."}, {"id": "20:18/q26/p5", "position": "Tapping branches instead of stripping them conserves grazing.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says it permits regrowth for others."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q27", "question": "How do sources compare Moses' answer with Muhammad's conduct?", "turns_on": "Some comparisons claim a difference in rank, while al-Ālūsī doubts their basis.", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q27/p1", "position": "Some read Moses' mention of the staff as lesser attention than Muhammad's focus on God and his community.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts created things with Muhammad's undistracted vision at 53:17, compares leaning with reliance on mercy at 8:64 and 5:67, cites a prayer of praise, and parses ومن اتبعك in 8:64 as included in God's sufficiency. Al-Ālūsī repeats the comparisons."}, {"id": "20:18/q27/p2", "position": "Al-Ālūsī says those comparisons have only a very slight basis.", "reasons": "He reports them to warn readers against being impressed."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q28", "question": "How is this staff episode connected with other passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q28/p1", "position": "The staff signs recur elsewhere and are compared with earlier scriptural accounts.", "reasons": "Study Quran names 27:10, 28:31 and Exodus 4:2; it also connects the inherited-staff lore with 7:106–108."}, {"id": "20:18/q28/p2", "position": "Other words and readings in the surrounding passage have their own parallels.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī contrasts Ibn ʿĀmir's readings of أشدد/أشركه with supplicatory readings and explains السيرة, الجناح, and جناح poetry; al-Farrāʾ glosses poetic لا نخفه as “do not reveal it.”"}, {"id": "20:18/q28/p3", "position": "The choice of “staff” rather than minsaʾa fits its merciful use for sheep.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts 34:14."}]}
{"id": "20:18/q29", "question": "What does the right hand in the preceding prompt denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:18/q29/p1", "position": "It first means the bodily right hand, with extended senses of strength and oath.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the lexical sequence for yamīn in God's prompt to Moses."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q01", "question": "How does qāla connect this speech to the preceding scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q01/p1", "position": "It resumes the narrative as the answer to an implied question about what God said next.", "reasons": "Bursevī identifies the implied question."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q02", "question": "What is Moses told to take, and with which hand?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports specify a hand in addition to identifying the serpent.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q02/p1", "position": "He is told to take the serpent, the transformed staff.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies the object pronoun as the serpent; Ibn al-Jawzī says it was still alive when taken."}, {"id": "20:21/q02/p2", "position": "He is told to take it specifically with his right hand.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabrisī state the right hand; al-Ālūsī attributes this specification to Wahb."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q03", "question": "How did Moses take the serpent and recover his staff?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over where Moses grasped the serpent and whether he first used a covering.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q03/p1", "position": "He put his bare hand into its mouth or onto its teeth or jaws, and it became the familiar wooden staff.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the teeth; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Qurṭubī and Study Quran report jaws or mouth. Al-Biqāʿī and Bursevī say his hand ended between the staff's prongs; Ibn al-Jawzī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya say touching or grasping it restored it. Al-Ālūsī finds direct taking more fitting for prophetic dignity."}, {"id": "20:21/q03/p2", "position": "He first tried to shield his hand with a cloak or sleeve, then uncovered it and took the serpent.", "reasons": "Wahb's versions say a wool cloak covered the hand; God or an angel asked whether it could protect him if God permitted harm, and Moses acknowledged human weakness. Al-Ṭabrisī places his hand in the mouth, between the prongs; al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya give a sleeve version. Al-Ālūsī finds this account less fitting than direct taking."}, {"id": "20:21/q03/p3", "position": "He grasped the serpent by its tail, and it became a staff.", "reasons": "Muqātil locates the grasp at the tail."}, {"id": "20:21/q03/p4", "position": "He was told to put his hand in its mouth, where it became a staff.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī presents this as one reported explanation alongside the view that it was a harmless prophetic sign."}]}
{"id": "20:21/q04", "question": "How many times was Moses called to take it before obeying?", "turns_on": "The divergent reports count earlier calls differently; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī assess their fit with prophetic dignity.", "positions": [{"id": "20:21/q04/p1", "position": "He obeyed after a third call, having failed to take it at two earlier calls.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Ṭabarī and al-Durr describes two earlier calls; Makkī gives three commands. Abū Ḥayyān objects that two refusals are unfitting for a prophet; al-Ālūsī doubts the report's soundness or fit with prophetic dignity."}, {"id": "20:21/q04/p2", "position": "He initially refused, then took it after a further command and assurance of safety.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās as transmitted in al-Durr links his flight, the renewed command, and the assurance that he was secure with 27:10 and 28:31."}, {"id": "20:21/q04/p3", "position": "He took it directly after God's command.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the direct-taking account better suits prophetic dignity; Abū Ḥayyān argues against repeated disobedience."}]}
